title: The Seventy-Two, the Good Samaritan, and Mary's Choice
summary: Jesus sends seventy-two disciples ahead of him in pairs to announce that the kingdom of God is near, warns the unrepentant towns of Galilee, and rejoices when they return. An expert in the law asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus answers his follow-up question, “And who is my neighbor?”, with the parable of the Good Samaritan. In a village Martha busily serves while her sister Mary sits at Jesus' feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the good portion.
story: Jesus has just set out for Jerusalem, and a Samaritan village has refused him. Now the mission widens: after the Twelve in chapter 9, a larger group is sent to prepare his way. Their success prompts Jesus' joyful prayer that the Father reveals himself to little children rather than to the wise. Then Luke sets side by side two scenes that together answer the question of eternal life: the Samaritan shows what it means to love one's neighbor, and Mary shows what it means to love God by listening to his word. The Samaritan hero lands with special force right after a Samaritan village turned Jesus away.
historical:
The manuscripts of Luke divide between seventy and seventy-two as the number sent out, and both are well attested. Either number may carry symbolism. Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek Septuagint, which would point to a mission reaching all peoples. Moses also appointed seventy elders to share his work (Numbers 11), and two more, Eldad and Medad, prophesied in the camp. Chorazin was a town in the hills just north of Capernaum; its ruins survive. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile ports that the prophets had denounced, and Jesus says even they would have repented.

The road from Jerusalem to Jericho ran about seventeen miles through rocky desert and dropped steeply, from Jerusalem's hill country to Jericho near the Jordan, well below sea level. Its ravines gave cover to robbers. Priests served in the temple in rotating groups and many lived in Jericho. Levites were members of the tribe of Levi who assisted the priests in the temple. On Samaritans and their hostility with Jews, see the note on 9:51-56.
cultural:
The missionaries' instructions assumed village hospitality: a household that received a traveler took on his care, and the greeting of peace was a blessing, not just a hello. Not greeting anyone on the road likely meant avoiding the long, elaborate greetings of the culture that would delay urgent work.

In the parable, a priest who touched a corpse became unclean (Leviticus 21:1-3), and the man lay half dead, perhaps impossible to tell from a dead man. Interpreters debate whether Jesus meant that concern for purity kept them away, or simply that they did not want to be bothered; the text gives no reason, and they are going down from Jerusalem, away from temple service. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them. Two denarii, about two days' wages, might cover a stay of several days, and the Samaritan's promise to return and pay more put himself at risk in a Jewish area. Sitting at someone's feet was the posture of a student (Paul uses the same phrase of his training under Gamaliel in Acts 22:3). For a woman to take that place among Jesus' disciples, rather than helping prepare the meal, broke with expectations.
literary: The dialogue with the lawyer has two rounds, each with a question from him, a counter-question from Jesus, an answer, and a command to act (“Do this and you will live” and “Go and do likewise”). His answer joins Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18, the same pairing Jesus himself gives in Mark 12:28-34 and Matthew 22:34-40. The parable reverses the lawyer's question. He asked whom he must count as a neighbor, looking for the limit; Jesus asks who acted as a neighbor, and the answer is the one he least expected. The parable is found only in Luke, as is the story of Martha and Mary, which is set right after it so that active love and attentive listening are held together. Martha's name repeated, “Martha, Martha”, is a gentle and affectionate rebuke.

outline.t: Jesus rejoices in the Father's revelation
The lawyer's question: love God and neighbor
The parable of the Good Samaritan

doctrines.note: The harvest is plentiful and workers are few, so the disciples pray for workers and go as workers. They go vulnerable, dependent on hospitality, carrying peace and the news that God's kingdom has come near.

The Law's heart is love for God with the whole self and love for neighbor as oneself. Jesus agrees with the lawyer's summary, then shows that the command cannot be fenced: a neighbor is anyone in need whom I can help.

In verses 21-22 Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and speaks to the Father, claiming a unique mutual knowledge: only the Father knows the Son, and only the Son knows the Father and reveals him. It is one of the clearest glimpses in the Synoptic Gospels of the Son's relationship with the Father.

words.note: Plesion, neighbor, literally the one near. In Leviticus 19:18 it mainly referred to a fellow Israelite, though Leviticus 19:34 extends the same love to the foreigner living among them. The lawyer wants to know who counts; Jesus makes the word describe how one acts.

Splagchnizomai, to be moved with compassion in one's inmost being. It is the turning point of the parable: the priest and Levite saw and passed by, the Samaritan saw and had compassion. Luke uses the same verb for Jesus at Nain (7:13) and for the father running to his son (15:20).

Eleos, mercy. In the Greek Old Testament it often renders the Hebrew hesed, God's loyal, covenant love. The lawyer cannot bring himself to say the Samaritan; he says the one who showed him mercy, which is exactly the point.

Hades, the Greek name for the realm of the dead, used to translate the Hebrew Sheol. Jesus' warning to Capernaum echoes Isaiah 14:13-15, where the proud king of Babylon, who hoped to climb to heaven, is brought down to the depths.

christ: Jesus sends messengers and says that to reject them is to reject him and the Father who sent him. He sees Satan fall from heaven as the kingdom advances. He speaks of knowing the Father as only the Son can, and says prophets and kings longed to see what the disciples now see. Some early interpreters, including Augustine, read the Good Samaritan as an allegory with Christ as the Samaritan, the wounded man as fallen humanity, and the inn as the church. That reading goes beyond what Jesus says: in context the parable answers a question about how to love one's neighbor. Yet the compassion the Samaritan shows is the same compassion Luke attributes to Jesus himself, and in Jesus the one who crosses every boundary to rescue the wounded is fully seen. Mary's choice points the same way: the one thing needed is to sit at the Lord's feet and hear his word.

hard.q: Does the lawyer's question, and Jesus' answer “Do this and you will live”, teach that eternal life is earned by keeping the law?
hard.a: Read alone, verse 28 sounds like salvation by works. Interpreters answer in different ways. Many Protestant readers, following Luther, hold that Jesus holds up the law's demand so the lawyer can see he has not met it, since no one loves God and neighbor perfectly; the lawyer's desire to justify himself shows he has not yet seen his need. Others, including many Catholic and Orthodox readers and some recent Protestant scholars, stress that Jesus is echoing Leviticus 18:5 and teaching that true faith always issues in love, so that those who inherit eternal life are marked by it. Both readings agree that Jesus does not lower the command. In Luke's larger story, eternal life comes through receiving Jesus and his forgiveness (as with the sinful woman in 7:50 or Zacchaeus in 19:9), and love of this kind is its fruit and evidence. The parable leaves the lawyer, and the reader, less concerned with defining the minimum and more aware of how far the command reaches.

questions: The lawyer asked who counts as his neighbor. Whom do you find it easiest to leave outside that category, and why?
The priest and the Levite had reasons to pass by. What reasons do you give yourself for not helping someone in need?
Martha was doing good work but was worried and upset about many things. What distracts you from the one thing needed, and what would sitting at Jesus' feet look like this week?
